blocks.text: “I declare,” he says, “I solemnly declare this. Until this crime is discovered and punished by the law, I almost feel as if there were a stain on my name. A gentleman gave a large part of his life to me. He gave the last day of his life to me. He constantly sat at my table and slept under my roof. He went from my house to his own house, and he was struck down within an hour of leaving my house. I cannot say that he was not followed from my house. He may have been watched at my house. He may even have been first picked out because of his connection with my house. That connection may have suggested that he had more money, and was altogether more important, than his own quiet and modest manner would have shown. I have money, I have influence, and I have a high position. If I cannot use them to bring everyone who took part in such a crime to light, then I fail. I fail to show my respect for that gentleman's memory. I fail to show my loyalty to a man who was always loyal to me.”

He makes this solemn statement with great feeling and seriousness. He looks round the room as if he were speaking to a large meeting. Meanwhile Mr. Bucket glances at him with a serious, watchful look. There might even be a touch of pity in that look—if such a thought were not too bold.

“The ceremony today,” Sir Leicester goes on, “showed very clearly how much respect the finest people in the land had for my dead friend.” He stresses the word “friend”, because death makes all people equal in rank. “I say that this has made the shock of this most horrible and shameless crime even worse. If it were my own brother who had committed it, I would not spare him.”
Mr. Bucket looks very serious. Volumnia says of the dead man that he was the most trustworthy and dearest person!
“You must feel it as a loss to you, miss,” Mr. Bucket replies in a calming voice. “No doubt about it. He was just the sort of man to be a loss, I'm sure he was.”

In her reply, Volumnia lets Mr. Bucket understand that her sensitive mind is fully decided. She will never get over it as long as she lives. Her nerves are ruined for ever. She does not expect to smile ever again. Meanwhile she folds a note into the shape of a cocked hat for that fearsome old general at Bath. The note describes her sad condition.
“It gives a delicate female a bad shock,” says Mr. Bucket kindly, “but it'll wear off.”

Volumnia wants more than anything to know what is being done. Are they going to convict that dreadful soldier, or whatever it is called? Did he have any accomplices—people who helped him—or whatever the thing is called in the law? And she asks a great deal more in the same simple, innocent way.

“Why, you see, miss,” Mr. Bucket answers. He brings his finger into action to persuade her. He is so naturally polite to ladies that he almost said “my dear”. “It ain't easy to answer those questions at the present moment. Not at the present moment. I've kept myself on this case, Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet”—Mr. Bucket brings Sir Leicester into the conversation because of his importance—“morning, noon, and night. Without a glass or two of sherry, I don't think I could have kept my mind working so hard as it has been. I could answer your questions, miss, but my duty forbids it. Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, will very soon be told everything that has been traced. And I hope that he may find it”—Mr. Bucket looks serious again—“to his satisfaction.”

The weak, tired cousin only hopes some fellow will be executed—as an example. He thinks that more influence is needed these days to get a man hanged than to get a man a job worth ten thousand a year. He has no doubt—as an example—that it is far better to hang the wrong fellow than no fellow at all.
